summary:
Belgorod Oblast stands under the national framework that Russia applies across all of its regions, and the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, assessment section updated 11 June 2025) sets out the conditions in force here. Same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment. The note records no region-specific findings; it states the national conditions that govern this region as it does every other.

Public expression is criminalised in terms that reach gender transition directly. 'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines of up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. The Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist makes participation punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years.

Enforcement is documented at scale. The Home Office note records that at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws between December 2022 and March 2024. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the designation, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal. The Supreme Court ruling entered into force in January 2024 and opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters.

Human Rights Watch further recorded that at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation between January 2024 and June 2025; two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention. A further 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles, and repeat displays are punishable under the criminal code by up to four years in prison. On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, an offence carrying up to 12 years.

The Home Office note assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. A foreign-government travel advisory for the country states that official support for travellers is 'very limited' in parts of the country.
tangentialFactors:
The extremist designation applies to supporters as well as LGBT people themselves, so displaying a symbol, attending an event or distributing material can attract liability independent of a visitor's own identity. Liability also reaches commercial activity: the 15 May 2025 charges against publishing-house staff concerned the sale of fiction, not advocacy.

Enforcement figures published by Human Rights Watch and the Home Office are national totals and are not disaggregated by region, so they describe the climate a visitor in Belgorod Oblast enters rather than a count of local cases. The foreign-government advisory's statement that official support is 'very limited' applies to parts of the country without identifying which parts.

The Home Office assessment standard matters beyond the visit: it is the benchmark used for UK asylum claims from people who leave Russia on account of their identity or advocacy.
localsOnly:
Residents of Belgorod Oblast have no legal route to change gender markers on official documents and no access to lawful gender-affirming care, both banned nationally in 2023. Same-sex marriage is prohibited.

No statute prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing or healthcare, so there is no domestic remedy for a resident dismissed, evicted or refused treatment on those grounds.

Residents face administrative fines for displaying banned symbols and, on repetition, criminal prosecution under the criminal code with up to four years' imprisonment; participation in the designated movement carries two to six years and organising six to ten years. At least 139 people were affected by anti-LGBT+ enforcement nationwide between December 2022 and March 2024, and 101 extremism-related convictions had been issued by 30 June 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports enforcement actions, raids, arrests or prosecutions specific to Belgorod Oblast; the dossier records the national legal framework and national enforcement totals that apply here, and local practice is not sourced.

The foreign-government advisory's reference to 'very limited' official support does not identify whether Belgorod Oblast falls within the parts of the country it describes.

Whether Belgorod Oblast's own authorities have issued regional directives on LGBT+ expression, or operate local venues or services relevant to trans visitors, is unresolved and not addressed by the inventory.
